Never runs anything from a directory the person did not mean and never shows a wrong path: every workspace the first version accepts is one where the root is unambiguous, and the harder cases are deferred into the follow-up documents the goal already asks for. A person who opens a multi-root workspace or a subfolder gets no pane content at all and must reopen the editor on the project's root, and the message they see depends on how the pane shows a failed or refused query (the Live query failure question); a project run from a subdirectory of a larger repository is refused outright.

Which folders: every workspace folder, each its own project with its own live missions. Folder to root: each folder's own path, used as given with no climbing. Override: none. The pane groups the missions by folder, `missions.py live` runs once per folder, and each mission's recipe lines run from the folder it was listed under. Multi-root workspaces are served in full, and a folder is taken exactly as the person opened it, so a project kept in a subdirectory of a larger repository and run from there works as its host CLI does. Inherits the subfolder hazard per folder: a folder below its root lists relative paths that are not the project's and scope reads that miss missions outside it; two folders of one repository list overlapping missions twice under different paths; the pane gains a per-folder grouping level and one `python3` start per folder on every refresh.

Which folders: every workspace folder. Folder to root: the git top level of each folder by `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, folders sharing one top level merged into one project. Override: none. The pane groups the missions by distinct root, `missions.py live` runs once per root, and each mission's recipe lines run from its own project's root. The most complete reading of the workspace: a multi-root workspace over several repositories shows every project, folders inside one repository collapse into it, and every path shown is the repo-relative path the plugin records. The heaviest option to build and test, a project grouping level on the page plus one `git` and one `python3` start per root on every refresh, and it carries the climbing mismatch for a project run from a subdirectory of a larger repository.

Which folders: every workspace folder that is its git work tree's top level, each its own project, every other folder taken as no project. Folder to root: the folder itself, never climbed, accepted only when it equals `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. Override: none. The pane groups the missions by folder and each mission's recipe lines run from its folder. Serves a multi-root workspace of several repositories opened at their roots while never guessing a root: no folder is reinterpreted, so no path is shown that the plugin's commits would not record. A subfolder is silently left out of the pane rather than shown, so a person who opened only subfolders sees nothing, and a project run from a subdirectory of a larger repository is excluded; it still pays the per-folder grouping level and the per-folder `git` and `python3` starts.

Which folders: one, chosen by the person from a quick pick listing the workspace folders whenever there is more than one, the choice kept in the extension's `workspaceState` and changeable through a command; a single-folder workspace needs no pick. The person states which project they mean, so a multi-root workspace never runs a line from a folder they did not intend, and a project run from a subdirectory of a larger repository can be picked as it is. Adds a prompt, stored state, and a command to change it, and a pick that goes stale (a folder removed from the workspace) needs handling; a folder picked below its root still gives the relative paths and narrowed scope reads of the as-is reading.

Which folders: one, chosen by the person from a quick pick of the workspace folders whenever there is more than one, kept in `workspaceState` and changeable through a command. Folder to root: the git top level of the chosen folder by `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. Override: the pick. `missions.py live` and every recipe line run from that top level. Combines an explicit choice among several folders with correct repo-relative paths when the chosen folder lies below its root, so neither ambiguity produces a wrong path. Carries both costs: the prompt, stored state, and change command of a pick, and the climbing mismatch for a project run from a subdirectory of a larger repository, which the pick cannot correct because the climb overrides it.

Which folders: the workspace folder holding the file of the active text editor (`workspace.getWorkspaceFolder` on `window.activeTextEditor`), read when the pane opens or refreshes, falling back to the first folder when no text editor is active. Folder to root: that folder's git top level by `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. Override: none. `missions.py live` and every recipe line run from that top level. Which folders: the one named by a VS Code setting holding the project root's path, resource- or workspace-scoped and empty by default; when it is empty, the first workspace folder. Override: the setting. `missions.py live` and every recipe line run from the root so chosen. The default handles the common subfolder case with correct paths, while the setting lets a person fix any case the default reads wrong, a project run from a subdirectory of a larger repository or a non-first folder of a multi-root workspace, with no prompt and with the choice kept in the workspace's own settings. open-question.question: Does the mission pane of the VS Code extension (`gurita-vscode`) come back by itself after the editor restarts, which needs a `WebviewPanelSerializer`, or does the person open it again?
open-question.recommendation: A run already ends with the editor and nothing is picked up after a restart, so a pane that ends with it behaves the same way. No serializer, activation event, or saved state has to be reconciled against missions that changed while the editor was closed, at the cost of one command per session.
open-question.alternative: The extension registers no `WebviewPanelSerializer` and does nothing at startup. The pane does not survive a restart or a window reload: VS Code drops a webview panel that has no serializer, and the person opens the pane again through the entry point the extension contributes. The new pane re-reads the live missions and draws its first page fresh, keeping no page or row state from before. It is the least to build and test: no serializer, no `onWebviewPanel:` activation event, no saved state to check against a mission or question that changed while the editor was closed. Since every run already ends with the editor and nothing is picked up after a restart, a pane that ends with it as well behaves the same way. After every restart, and after every window reload, the pane is gone from the editor area and has to be opened again, a small step the person takes each session. How small depends on what entry point the sibling question on pane opening settles on.

The extension registers a `WebviewPanelSerializer` for its one view type under an `onWebviewPanel:<viewType>` activation event. A pane that was open at shutdown comes back in its editor column after a restart or reload. `deserializeWebviewPanel` ignores the saved state and sets the panel up exactly as the open command does, re-reading the live missions and drawing the default page with every question row closed. A pane that was closed at shutdown stays closed. The pane is where the person left it without being opened again, and none of the extra code reads back old state, so nothing restored can name a mission that has since finished or a question that has since been answered. The deserialize path is the open command's own setup applied to a panel VS Code hands over. It adds a serializer, an activation event, and a second way the one panel comes into being that has to be tested beside the open command. The person still loses which mission's page they were on and which rows they had opened, so on a project with several live missions they move back to their page by hand after every restart.

The extension registers a `WebviewPanelSerializer` as above, and the page saves through `setState` which mission's page it shows and which question rows are open. After a restart or reload, `deserializeWebviewPanel` receives that state, re-reads the live missions and the question document, and draws the saved mission's page with the saved rows open. A mission no longer live falls back to the default page, and a row whose question no longer stands is dropped. A pane closed at shutdown stays closed. The person comes back to exactly the page and open rows they left, which is all the serializer's state handoff exists for. The same saved state may also be what keeps the rows across a hidden pane, so the restart costs little beyond the serializer. The most to build and test: the saved state has to be checked against missions and questions that may have changed while the editor was closed, with a fallback for each. How much of the state comes free depends on how the sibling question on page redraw keeps the opened rows. If they are kept in the extension's memory rather than through `setState`, they have to be mirrored into the page's state for this option alone.

The extension registers no serializer. It activates at startup in a workspace that holds a live mission (a `workspaceContains` event on the mission discovery pattern, or `onStartupFinished` followed by the `live` query) and opens the pane, drawn fresh, whether or not it was open before the restart or reload. This rejects the premise that coming back by itself needs a serializer. In a project with missions the pane is always there after a restart, a reload, or a fresh first open of the folder, with no serializer and no saved state to reconcile, and the person never has to look for how to open it. It opens an editor tab the person may have closed on purpose, every session, and activates the extension at every startup in such a project. Whether this is part of how the pane opens at all belongs to the sibling question on pane opening, so this option holds only if that question leaves room for an automatic open.

The extension registers a `WebviewPanelSerializer` restoring the saved page state (the mission page shown and the open question rows, checked against what is live now) for a pane that was open at shutdown. It also opens the pane, drawn fresh, at startup in a workspace that holds a live mission when no pane was restored. The pane is always present in a project with missions, and when it was open before it comes back on the page and rows the person left. It carries the whole cost of both mechanisms, a serializer with state reconciliation and a startup activation, and it still reopens a pane the person closed. It also depends on the sibling question on pane opening leaving room for an automatic open, and on how the sibling question on page redraw keeps the opened rows.

open-question.question: Does a click on a recipe button in the VS Code extension (`gurita-vscode`), other than the looped task recipe with its preview, start the run at once, or does the page first show the lines it is about to run and wait for a confirmation?
open-question.recommendation: A routine click stays one act, as the draft's run once per click reads, while the lines under each button show which hosts, models, and efforts it is about to spend, as the draft says a button can. The display is static text needing no pending state, and a wrong answer is one commit to revert.
open-question.alternative: No confirmation step, but the lines are visible before the click. Every recipe button on the page carries its recipe's lines, as written with their placeholders, in a row that can be expanded under the button or in its hover text, so the person can read them before clicking. The click itself starts the runner at once, as in a click with no confirmation, and adds no dialog, page state, or second click. The person can check what a button runs whenever they want, which keeps the draft's "a button can show the lines it is about to run", and a routine click still costs one act. The display is static page content drawn from the recipe text the extension already reads. It needs no pending state to survive a redraw. Reading is optional, so the accidental or wrong-row click this is meant to catch still starts the run unseen. Placeholders are shown unfilled, so the values the click will fix, such as the Short Title or a typed answer, are never shown before the run. It also puts the full text of every shipped and own recipe on the page beside its button.

No confirmation step for any recipe. A click on any recipe button, whether a chain button on a mission's page, a per-question button in the question view, or one of the two mission-start buttons once its input boxes are filled, starts the runner in its terminal immediately. Nothing about the lines is shown on the page before or at the click, and the terminal shows each line as the runner starts it. The only way back is ending the runner, which ends the line it is running, or reverting the commits that line made. It is the least to build and the least to click: a recipe click is one act, as the draft's "run once per click from its first line to its last" reads. The person picked the button, and its values were already fixed by the click or typed into an input box. Each recorded step is one commit, so a wrong run is undone by revert-then-re-answer, which the workflow already uses to correct a bad answer. A mis-click on a chain starts several headless model runs. Every shipped line carries `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, and each run spends quota and lands commits before the person has seen what it will do. A per-question button clicked on the wrong row records an answer for the wrong question. The constraint's promise that "a button can show the lines it is about to run" goes unused.

A confirmation step for every recipe the question covers: the chains, the six one-line button recipes (the two interactive discuss lines included), and every recipe of the person's own, with no setting to switch it off. The page shows the confirmation itself, in the same place and manner as the looped recipe's preview. A click shows the recipe's lines, each with the values the click fixed shown in place of its placeholders, under a Run control and a Cancel control. The runner starts only on Run, and nothing is started or written on Cancel. Every run is preceded by the exact lines and values it will run with. That catches a wrong recipe, a wrong question row, and a typo in a typed answer before any model run or commit. Clicking works the same way everywhere, the looped recipe included, so the person learns one flow and the page holds one kind of pre-run view. Every run costs a second click, the routine ones included: a further requirements iteration clicked round after round, or an interactive discuss line that only opens a conversation and writes nothing by itself. The page gains a pending state that has to be kept, or dropped knowingly, when the page is redrawn or the pane is hidden, which depends on how the page-redraw sibling settles. The values are shown as display text only, since the run receives them through the session's environment and never in the line's text.

A confirmation step for every recipe the question covers, as in the always-on page confirmation, with no setting, but shown through VS Code's own modal message (`showWarningMessage` or `showInformationMessage` with `modal: true`) rather than on the page. The message's detail text lists the recipe's lines with the values the click fixed shown in place of their placeholders, a Run button starts the runner, and dismissing the dialog starts nothing. Every run is confirmed against its lines and values, using a native, blocking dialog that is a single API call. The page gains no pending state, so the confirmation is independent of how the page is redrawn or kept while hidden, and the dialog cannot be missed or left half-open. A modal's detail text is plain, unformatted, and wrapped, and the shipped chain lines are long, each with its host binary, model, effort, and permission flag. A five-line chain therefore reads poorly in it. It looks and behaves differently from the looped recipe's on-page preview, and like any always-on confirmation it costs a second click on every routine run.

A confirmation step for every recipe the question covers, with no setting. The confirmation is in the run's terminal, not on the page or in a dialog. The click starts the runner at once. Before it runs any line, the runner prints the chain's lines with the values its session holds filled in, then waits for Enter to go on. Ending the terminal, or answering no, runs nothing. Started by hand outside the editor, the runner prompts the same way unless an argument of its own skips the prompt. The lines are confirmed where they will run, with the values as the session really holds them, not as a display rendering. The confirmation needs no page state and no dialog. It also guards a hand start of the runner the same way, from the one file that already holds the chain logic. The runner gains an interactive prompt and a mode argument to skip it, which makes it harder to run as a plain non-interactive script. A chain is left waiting in a terminal the person may not have looked at, and the person moves focus from the page to the terminal for every run. Like any always-on confirmation, it costs a second act on every routine run.

A confirmation step that depends on the kind of line. On the page, as the looped preview is shown, a confirmation with the filled lines and Run and Cancel controls comes before every recipe that holds at least one headless line, by the runner's own rule: an unmarked line holding a `gurita:` invocation. That covers every chain and the four headless one-line button recipes (the three answer recipes and `define-mission-goal`). A recipe whose only skill lines are interactive, such as the `discuss-open-question` and `discuss-mission-goal` buttons, starts at once, because it opens a terminal conversation that the person steers. There is no setting. Confirmation falls exactly on the runs that act unattended and land commits, and it guards the one-line answer buttons, where a wrong row or a wrong alternative records a wrong decision. It is skipped where the person is about to take over a conversation anyway and nothing is written without them. The kind test reuses the line classification the runner already makes. Clicking behaves two ways, and the page must classify each recipe's lines before it can decide. Every routine chain click, a repeated requirements iteration included, still costs a second click. The pending confirmation state on the page depends on how the page-redraw sibling settles.

A confirmation step that depends on how long the recipe is. On the page, as the looped preview is shown, a confirmation with the filled lines and Run and Cancel controls comes before every recipe of more than one line: the shipped chains and any multi-line recipe of the person's own. Every one-line recipe starts at once: the six button recipes (per-question answers, the discuss lines, and the define line) and any one-line own recipe. There is no setting. The costly, many-run chains, the ones a mis-click turns into several unattended model runs and commits, get a pause. The per-question and mission-start buttons, where the person has just picked a question and alternative or typed an input and each run is one commit easy to revert, stay one click. The rule is a line count, not a classification. A one-line headless answer button records a decision with no chance to check that it is the right row or the right alternative. A one-line own recipe that wraps a costly line skips the pause because of how it is written. Every routine chain click still costs a second click, and the pending state on the page depends on how the page-redraw sibling settles.

Configurable confirmation. On the page, as the looped preview is shown, a confirmation with the filled lines and Run and Cancel controls comes before every recipe the question covers, while a VS Code user setting is on. The setting is on by default. With it off, every recipe click starts the runner at once. A new user, or the maintainer's first runs of a new extension, gets the safe behaviour: each run checked against its lines and values. Once the person trusts their recipes, they can drop the second click for good with one switch, so neither safety nor speed is forced on everyone. It adds a second user setting beside the own-recipe path setting, and the extension must document and test it. It also makes both click behaviours permanent parts of the extension. A person who turns it off is back to a mis-click starting chains with skipped permissions. The pending state on the page depends on how the page-redraw sibling settles.

Configurable confirmation, off by default. Every recipe click starts the runner at once unless a VS Code user setting, off by default, is turned on. With the setting on, a confirmation on the page, as the looped preview is shown, with the filled lines and Run and Cancel controls, comes before every recipe the question covers. The default is the one-click flow the draft describes, and the maintainer, the first and likely only user, who already runs these lines by hand, pays no extra click. A person who wants a pause can still have one without changing any recipe. It adds a setting and two click behaviours to build and test for a pause that is off unless someone looks for it. In the default state every risk of an immediate run remains: a wrong-row answer, or a mis-clicked chain of permission-skipping model runs.

open-question.question: The mission pane of the VS Code extension (`gurita-vscode`) holds one page per live mission, and a way on the pane itself moves between the missions. By what control does a person move from one mission's page to another's, and which mission's page does the pane show when it is opened while several missions are live?
open-question.recommendation: Live missions are few, two when the draft measured, so a tab row keeps every one in view and one click away, with the two mission-starting buttons at its end where the draft places them. Opening on the first mission in the `live` order needs no stored state and no fallback for a mission that has finished, at the cost of one click when the mission in use sorts later.
open-question.alternative: A row of tabs across the top of the pane, one per live mission in the order `missions.py live` prints them, each tab showing the mission's title with its path as a tooltip, the selected tab's page shown beneath and the two mission-starting buttons at the row's end; clicking a tab switches the page in place. When opened, the pane shows the page of the first mission in `live`'s path order, holding no memory of an earlier choice, and after a refresh it stays on the page shown unless that mission is no longer live, when it falls back to the first. Every live mission stays visible and one click away on every page, and the opening page needs no stored state, so it is deterministic from the `live` print alone and nothing can go stale. The pane always opens on whichever mission sorts first by path, not the one the person was working on, so with several missions live a person working on a later one switches by hand on every opening, and the tab row crowds or wraps when many missions are live or titles are long.

The same row of tabs, one per live mission in `live`'s path order with the start buttons at its end, and the pane opens on the mission whose page the person last showed, its path kept by the extension in its per-workspace storage (`workspaceState`) on each switch, so it outlives the panel's closing and the editor's restart; when that path is no longer live, or none is stored, it opens on the first mission in path order. Reopening the pane returns the person to the mission they were working on, which is what a sitting over one mission among several wants, while every other mission stays one click away on the tab row. The extension gains a piece of state of its own beside the documents it re-reads, kept per workspace and needing a fallback for a finished or renamed mission, against the draft's lean toward reading everything from the project; the tab row still crowds when many missions are live.

One dropdown (a `<select>`) at the top of the pane listing the live missions in `live`'s path order, each entry its title and path, with the two mission-starting buttons beside it; choosing an entry switches the page in place. When opened, the pane shows the first mission in path order, holding no memory of an earlier choice, and after a refresh it keeps the page shown unless that mission is no longer live. A single compact control takes the same space however many missions are live and shows full titles and paths without crowding, the simplest switch to build, with an opening page deterministic from `live` alone. The other missions are hidden until the dropdown is opened, so switching takes two clicks and the person does not see at a glance which missions are live, and the pane opens on the first mission by path rather than the one in use.

The same dropdown of live missions in `live`'s path order with the start buttons beside it, and the pane opens on the mission last shown, its path kept in the extension's per-workspace storage (`workspaceState`) on each switch, falling back to the first mission in path order when the stored path is no longer live or none is stored. The compact control that does not crowd with many missions, combined with reopening on the mission the person was working on, so the extra click of a dropdown is rarely needed. Combines the dropdown's hidden list and two-click switch with a piece of extension-held state that needs its own fallback, the two costs of the other options together for the sake of their two benefits.

The pane opens on an overview page of its own listing every live mission in `live`'s path order, each entry its title, path, and the page's state label, with the two mission-starting buttons standing there; clicking an entry shows that mission's page, which carries a back control to the overview at its top, so moving between missions passes through the overview. The pane always opens on the overview whenever more than one mission is live, holding no stored choice. The overview shows every live mission's state side by side, the one view of the whole project's missions the pane would otherwise not give, and the opening page needs no stored state and never presumes which mission the person wants. Every opening and every switch costs an extra click through the overview, and the start buttons and the overview sit apart from the mission pages, so a mission page needs a header of its own to keep the start buttons beside the way between missions as the draft places them.

The same overview page listing every live mission with its title, path, and state label, the start buttons on it, and a back control at the top of each mission page; the pane opens on the mission page last shown, its path kept in the extension's per-workspace storage (`workspaceState`), and on the overview when the stored path is no longer live or none is stored. Reopening returns straight to the mission in use while the overview still gives the side-by-side view of every mission's state one click away. Carries both the extension-held state and its fallback and the overview's extra click on every switch between missions, the most parts to build of any option for a first version meant to be the least to build.

open-question.question: A mission's page in the VS Code extension (`gurita-vscode`) draws its question view and its label from the extension's own parse of that mission's `open_questions.xml`, and its remaining tasks from the `##` headings of `TASKS_TODO.md`. What does the page show when one of those two files is missing or cannot be parsed, as when a merge left conflict markers in the question document?
open-question.recommendation: Each section and each label fact comes from one of the two files, so a notice standing in place of what the failed file feeds, with its path and the parser's own message, keeps everything that did read usable and shows the rest as unknown, never as a false converged state. The cause is quoted and nothing is classified, as the plugin's own stops do.
open-question.alternative: The failure is confined to the part of the page drawn from the file that failed. If `open_questions.xml` is missing or does not parse (conflict markers included), the question view, its row and alternative buttons, and the question facts of the label are replaced by one notice. The notice names the file's path, says whether it is missing or unparsable, and quotes the parser's own message. If `TASKS_TODO.md` is missing, or holds a conflict-marker line (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` at column 0), the remaining-task headings and the label's tasks-remain fact get the same kind of notice. Everything else is drawn as usual: the path, the title, and `started` or `defined` from `missions.py live`, the label facts and section that come from the file that did read, and every recipe button. On the next re-read the notice goes away once the file reads again. The person still sees and can use every part of the page that is correct, and is told exactly which file broke and why. Facts from the broken file read as unknown rather than as a false state, which fits the draft's rule that the label holds only what the documents say now and gates no button. The page and label need an unknown state for each of the two files, so there are more cases to build and test than an all-or-nothing page needs. A recipe button stays offered beside a document the extension could not read, so a click leads to the skill's own stop line rather than being caught on the page.

If either file is missing or cannot be read (the same conditions as above: unparsable XML, or a conflict-marker line in `TASKS_TODO.md`), the mission's page drops the question view, the remaining-task headings, and the whole label, readable file included. In their place it shows one notice naming each file that failed, whether it is missing or unparsable, and the parser's message. The page keeps its path, title, and `started` or `defined` from `missions.py live`, and every recipe button, since the label gates none. The full page comes back on the first re-read after both files read again. The page has only two states, whole or broken, so no partial label or half-drawn page has to be designed. A broken mission is impossible to miss, and nothing it shows rests on a document it could not read in full. A broken `TASKS_TODO.md` also hides a question view that read correctly, and the other way round, so the person loses correct information until both files are fixed. Leaving recipe buttons on a page that otherwise shows only an error looks inconsistent.

Only a document that is present but unparsable counts as a failure. A missing `open_questions.xml` is read as an empty question list and a missing `TASKS_TODO.md` as no remaining tasks. The task headings are read line by line whatever the file holds, so a `TASKS_TODO.md` with conflict markers shows the `##` headings from both sides. An `open_questions.xml` that does not parse gets a notice in its own section: path, `unparsable`, and the parser's message in place of the question view and the label's question facts. The rest of the page and every recipe button are drawn as usual. It is the least to build. Only the XML parse can fail, which is the one read that really parses, and the task read keeps the leniency the task-list tool shows when it accepts any file. A deleted question document makes the label say the question list is empty, a converged state that the open-question tool's own `list` would refuse with an `Error:` line. A conflicted task list shows duplicate or merged headings as if they were real tasks, so the page can claim a state the documents do not hold.

The page has no failure state of its own. Any file that is missing or does not parse is drawn as if it held nothing: no question rows, no remaining-task headings, and label facts computed from those empty readings. A parse error is only kept from crashing the page or the extension. No notice is shown, and recipe buttons stay offered as always, so the skills' stop lines are the only place a broken document shows up. This is final, not a step to add handling later. Nothing has to be built beyond keeping a parse error from breaking the pane, which suits an experimental first version whose user is the maintainer, who already knows when a merge has left markers. A broken document looks exactly like a converged mission with nothing left to do, which is the most misleading thing the page could show.
